title: The Unwilling Suspension of Belief: Critical Thinking and Writing in Tension
author: Terry Underwood, PhD
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn (Substack)
summary: Terry Underwood, PhD, presents a research-grounded argument that fluent writing and critical thinking are distinct cognitive activities — and that a 2004 study from Washington State University proved this chasm long before AI made it an emergency. The central evidence is Condon and Kelly-Riley's finding that WSU's highly reliable writing placement instrument inversely correlated with critical thinking scores: the better the writing, the lower the critical thinking (r = -0.339, P = .015). A faculty workshop crystallized the gap when twenty-five instructors rated the same freshman paper as acceptable writing yet only a '2 on a six-point' critical thinking scale, and concluded the shortfall originated in what they had asked students to do rather than what students could do. AAC&U; rubric analysis reinforces the finding: the Written Communication rubric can be satisfied entirely by fluent, audience-aware prose that interrogates nothing, while the Critical Thinking rubric requires a posture of earned and deferred judgment that writing never entails. The arrival of LLMs is framed not as a new crisis but as an unintended replication of the WSU study — machines that produce Capstone-level prose with zero interrogation have industrialized a counterfeit that always existed. Danielle Ozaki's student voice ('having to think about it, instead of just write it, took some getting used to') anchors the article as a through-line, demonstrating that even competent writers experienced critical thinking as friction deliberately introduced into a process that had run smoothly without it. Underwood closes with an urgent call: the field has never had a stable shared definition of critical thinking, and AI has now made the cost of that gap impossible to ignore.
points: WSU's Condon and Kelly-Riley (2004) found a statistically significant inverse correlation between writing assessment scores and critical thinking scores (r = -0.339, P = .015), meaning the placement system had for years been certifying good writers while systematically passing over poor thinkers.

The AAC&U; Written Communication rubric can be satisfied in full without any critical thinking — a writer who attends accurately to audience, conventions, and sources earns every Capstone mark while doing no interrogation — because CT is 'permitted by the Writing rubric; it is never entailed.'

LLMs constitute an unintended replication of the WSU study: they produce fluent, conventionally sound, audience-aware prose with no interrogation behind it, exposing the conflation of writing and critical thinking that organized instruction for decades and revealing that the counterfeit was always present.

In courses where faculty explicitly used the WSU Guide to Rating Critical Thinking, student CT scores increased 'up to three and a half times as much' as students in ordinary progression — proving critical thinking is learnable when explicitly demanded rather than assumed to arrive through writing practice alone.

WSU faculty admitted they were 'satisfied with accurate information retrieval and summary' and had not actively elicited thinking skills in assignments — the shortfall originated in what faculty asked for, not in what students were capable of, a diagnosis with direct implications for AI-era pedagogy.
quotes: We are currently panicking over AI's ability to write perfect essays, but two decades ago, an overlooked study demonstrated convincingly that fluent writing never actually guaranteed deep thought. Danielle Ozaki put her finger on precisely what had been nagging the writing faculty at Washington State University for some time before the transformation. Like most writing people, they had bought the popular assumption that writing is thinking, even critical thinking.

Across sixty paired samples, 'the better the writing, the lower the critical thinking score, but the more problematic the writing, the higher the critical thinking score.' Students 'deemed better prepared for the rigors of academic writing' by the placement exam scored lower on critical thinking 'at a statistically significant level (r = -0.339, P = .015).'

A student could earn every Capstone mark vis a vis responsive to audience, fluent, masterful with conventions while doing no critical thinking at all. CT is permitted by the Writing rubric; it is never entailed.

Large language models produce fluent, conventionally sound, audience-aware prose with no interrogation behind it: no assumptions surfaced, no experts questioned, no judgment deferred. The AAC&U; Written Communication rubric applies nicely.

Writing offered CT a doorway into information literacy, i.e., judging the quality of sources, but little more; CT requires expression yet declines to interrogate its dependence on writing. Writing teachers persist in asserting that they are teaching critical thinking, but are they?

'Having to think about it, instead of just write it, took some getting used to.' Read again after the AAC&U; rubrics, Danielle's sentence stops being a charming aside and becomes a stunning piece of evidence. She names two activities and insists they are different: writing it and thinking about it.

Critical thinking, it turned out, did not casually arrive on its own; it showed up when explicitly demanded. Where faculty did overtly use the Guide in their teaching, thinking rose sharply, with students increasing their scores up to three and a half times as much as those moving through the ordinary freshman-to-junior progression.

We've never had a stable, shared definition of critical thinking. Faculty, he found, largely could not 'describe or define critical thinking beyond trendy pedagogical buzz words,' even as the overwhelming majority called it central to their teaching.

Much of what we call critical writing is interrogation in form only: a student restates a novel's plot, appreciates its themes, and earns the grade without ever questioning an assumption or weighing a rival reading. The distinction that matters is not fact versus fiction.
